claims.text: Equimolar CoCrFeNiTi has relatively low hardness and strength despite good ductility and machinability.
The low hardness and strength of equimolar CoCrFeNiTi are controlled by an absence of nanoscale chemical short-range order or incipient ordering.
Nanoscale CSRO or B2-like clusters normally act as barriers to dislocation motion.
A controlled aging treatment can induce CSRO in equimolar CoCrFeNiTi without producing secondary-phase precipitation.
The starting material is an as-cast, single-phase equimolar CoCrFeNiTi solid solution.
Aging between 400 and 600 °C can be calibrated to enhance chemical ordering while retaining a single-phase state.
Aging produces nanoscale CSRO or incipient B2-type ordered clusters.
CSRO produces local compositional fluctuations that impede dislocation motion.
B2 ordering is associated with a distinct dislocation-mediated deformation mode involving superdislocations.
In the unaged, chemically disordered state, relatively unhindered dislocation glide causes lower hardness and yield strength.
A moderate degree of chemical order raises resistance to plastic deformation by creating dislocation barriers.
Aging can increase nanoindentation hardness relative to the as-cast state.
Aging-induced CSRO will increase the yield strength of CoCrFeNiTi.
The hardness and yield-strength increases will persist from room temperature to 600 °C.
The strength increase will occur with only a modest reduction in plasticity, leaving acceptable ductility.
Any predicted mechanical improvement is caused specifically by CSRO rather than by secondary-phase precipitation.
The untreated baseline has a homogeneous, chemically disordered solid-solution microstructure.
The proposed comparison uses an untreated as-cast control and specimens aged at 500 °C for 1, 5, or 10 hours.
Nanoindentation, compression or tensile testing, TEM, and atom-probe tomography are used to correlate mechanical changes with nanoscale chemical order.
